---
title: "6.4 Poisson Regression Example"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

## Software considerations

- Convergence (of the maximum likelihood estimates) is usually fast and problems are rarely encountered
  - Also true for negative binomial model (covered next)
- Convergence can be trickier for zero-inflated count models (covered end of this section)
  - But, lack of convergence generally indicates that model is not a good fit for your data and solution is to use a regular count model

## Example

- Add Health Wave IV
  - DV: Number of drinks consumed in a typical sitting
  - IVs: Gender, Age (24 -- 33)
  - Controls: Education, race, income, marital status, parental status

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_ah4", clear

*6.4.a
hist drinktime, percent fcolor(none) xlab(0(2)18) ///
    title("[6.4.a] Distribution of Number of Drinks Consumed in a Typical Sitting")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-06_04_a-drinks-01.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-06_04_a-drinks-01.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.a] Histogram of the average number of drinks in a sitting, from 0 to 18: about 42% report 0 drinks, about 10% 1, 15% 2, 11% 3, and few report more than 6."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[6.4.a] Histogram of the average number of drinks in a sitting, from 0 to 18: about 42% report 0 drinks, about 10% 1, 15% 2, 11% 3, and few report more than 6."
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(modelsummary)    # regression tables
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

ah4 <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_ah4.dta")

# 6.4.a
ggplot(ah4, aes(x = drinktime)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(100 * count / sum(count))), binwidth = 1,
    fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 18, 2)) +
  labs(title = "[6.4.a] Distribution of Number of Drinks Consumed in a Typical Sitting",
    x = "Average Drinks Each Time", y = "Percent")
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*6.4.b
poisson drinktime i.woman c.age i.college i.race c.income ///
    i.spouserole i.parrole
est store pmod
est table pmod, ///
    title("[6.4.b] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting") ///
    b(%5.3f) star(.05 .01 .001)
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# Keep model variables; drop any missing data
ah4 <- ah4[c("drinktime", "woman", "age", "college", "race", "income", "spouserole",
  "parrole")]
ah4 <- ah4[complete.cases(ah4), ]

# Treat binary/nominal variables as factors
ah4 <- ah4 |>
  mutate(across(c(woman, college, race, spouserole, parrole), as_factor))

# 6.4.b
pmod <- glm(drinktime ~ woman + age + college + race + income + spouserole + parrole,
  family = "poisson", data = ah4)

modelsummary(pmod, stars = c("*" = .05, "**" = .01, "***" = .001),
  title = "[6.4.b] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting")
```

:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
In Stata, use the [**poisson**](https://www.stata.com/manuals13/rpoisson.pdf) command

In R, use [**glm**](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/glm) and specify family = "poisson"

Poisson regression coefficients are in the metric of the log rate---which is not very useful

We usually exponentiate the coefficients and interpret in terms of the factor change on the rate (see below)
:::

## Factor change in the rate E(y | x)

- To go from log rates to rates metric, we exponentiate the coefficients
  - This makes the coefficients multiplicative effects
- The effect of a change in *x~k~* does not depend on values of the *x*'s

> ***Factor change interpretation**: For a unit change in x~k~ the expected count (rate) changes by a factor of exp(β~k~), holding other variables constant*

### Interpreting factor changes in rate

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*6.4.c - Exponentiated coefs with irr option
qui poisson drinktime i.woman c.age i.college i.race c.income ///
    i.spouserole i.parrole, irr
est table pmod, ///
    title("[6.4.c] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting (exponentiated coefficients = IRRs)") ///
    b(%5.3f) star(.05 .01 .001) eform
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# 6.4.c - Exponentiated coefficients
exp(coef(pmod))
```

:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
Exponentiated coefficients are referred to as "incident rate ratios" in Poisson
:::

> - *Women's rates of drinking are lower than men's by a factor of about 0.61*
> - *Each additional year of age is associated with a 0.95 times decrease in the number of drinks consumed in a sitting*
> - *Black and Asian respondents drink fewer drinks in a sitting than do White respondents (e^b^ = 0.69; e^b^ = 0.88); in contrast, Native American respondents drink 1.33 times more drinks in a sitting than White respondents*
> - *An additional \$1000 of income is associated with consuming 1.003 times more drinks in a sitting*

## Plots of the predicted rate

- The predicted rate is the default quantity with **margins** in Stata and with **plot_predictions** in R
  - Easy to calculate

$$E(y) = \widehat{\mu} = \exp(\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol{\beta})$$

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*6.4.e
qui margins, at(age=(24(1)33) woman=(0 1))
marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(0(1)4) ///
    ytitle("Number of Drinks") xtitle("Age in Years") ///
    title("[6.4.e] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Age", size(medium))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-06_04_e-drinks-06.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-06_04_e-drinks-06.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.e] Predicted number of drinks in a sitting by age, with confidence intervals: men's predictions fall from about 3.3 at age 24 to 2.1 at age 33, and women's from about 2.0 to 1.3."}

## R

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
R's **plot_predictions** default would hold controls at modal person. To get average predictions, need the **newdata** statement with a "counterfactual" **grid_type.**
:::

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[6.4.e] Predicted number of drinks in a sitting by age, with confidence intervals: men's predictions fall from about 3.3 at age 24 to 2.1 at age 33, and women's from about 2.0 to 1.3."
# 6.4.e
plot_predictions(pmod, by = c("age", "woman"),
  newdata = datagrid(age = 24:33, woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 24:33) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:4, limits = c(0, 4)) +
  labs(title = "[6.4.e] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Age",
    x = "Age in Years", y = "Number of Drinks", color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[6.4.g] Predicted number of drinks by age from 0 to 100, far beyond the observed ages: the curve falls steeply from about 9 at age 0 and flattens near 0 by age 80, showing the exponential form of the model."
# Show nonlinearities (predictions across a broader range)
# 6.4.g
plot_predictions(pmod, by = "age",
  newdata = datagrid(age = seq(0, 100, 2.5), grid_type = "counterfactual"), vcov = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2), limits = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(title = "[6.4.g] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Age",
    x = "Age in Years", y = "Number of Drinks")
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[6.4.h] Predicted number of drinks by personal income from 0 to $2,000,000, far beyond the observed incomes: the curve is nearly flat at first and then rises steeply to about 600 drinks, showing the exponential form of the model."
# 6.4.h
plot_predictions(pmod, by = "income",
  newdata = datagrid(income = seq(0, 2000, 50), grid_type = "counterfactual"), vcov = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 2000, 250)) +
  labs(title = "[6.4.h] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Income",
    x = "Personal Income in $1000s", y = "Number of Drinks")
```

:::

## Marginal effect on the rate

- The factor change (*e^b^*) is constant; it does not differ across values of the IVs
- The marginal effect depends on the values of the IVs
  - Considerations about what starting and ending values to use; whether to hold control variables at the mean (MEM) or to average over observed values (AMEs) are identical in count models to other nonlinear models

$$ME = \eta(x_{k} = end,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*}) - \eta(x_{k} = start,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*})$$

- There are multiple potential predictions of interest with count models
  - Can define $\eta$ as the rate (AKA expected count; AKA \# of expected "events")
  - Can define $\eta$ as the Pr(*y* = *j*)
  - Can define $\eta$ as the probability of a range of outcomes, e.g., Pr(*y* = 4,5,6,7, or 8)
- For marginal effects on the rate/count:

> ***Interpretation:** The difference in the expected count for a change in x~k~ of δ, holding other independent variables constant*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare woman, model(pmod)
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
avg_comparisons(pmod, variables = "woman")
```

:::

> *On average, women consume about one fewer drink in a typical sitting than do men (ME = -1.038; p \< 0.001).*

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
**Interpretation tip**: Count DVs tend to have a natural metric; using it in your interpretations instead of "rate" or "expected count" is recommended. Here, "number of drinks".
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
With [**mecompare**](https://www.trentonmize.com/software/mecompare/examples/model-types.html), can customize **start()** place of change, and the **amount(#)** of change. **uncenter** the change if you want an ME between those two exact \#s.
:::

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare age, model(pmod) start(age=25) amount(5) uncenter
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
avg_comparisons(pmod, variables = list(age = c(25, 30)))
```

:::

> *Aging from 25 to 30 is associated with consuming about ½ a drink less per sitting (ME = -0.562; p \< 0.001).*

## Probabilities of specific counts

- For a given rate, the probability of count *j* for observation *i* is:

$$\Pr(y_{i} = j\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \frac{e^{-\widehat{\mu}_{i}}\,\widehat{\mu}_{i}^{\,j}}{j!}$$

- Sometimes the probability of specific count is of interest
  - Pr(*y* = 0) is commonly of interest
  - Depending on research question, probabilities at other values and/or cumulative probabilities may be of interest
    - E.g., To determine who is at risk, examine what the probability is that someone consumes ≥ 4 drinks in a typical sitting: Pr(*y* ≥ 4)
- Probabilities are also used to assess the adequacy of the model

### Plotting probabilities of specific counts

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

- In Stata, can request the probability of a specific count \# on **margins**, with option **predict(pr(#))**
  - And a range with **predict(pr(#,#))**

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*6.4.i - Pr(y=0)
qui margins, at(age=(21(1)35) woman=(0 1)) predict(pr(0))
marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(0(.1).4) xlab(21(2)35) ///
    ytitle("Pr(Typically Consumes 0 Drinks)") xtitle("Age in Years") ///
    title("[6.4.i] Probability of Consuming Zero Drinks in a Typical Sitting", size(medium))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-06_04_i-drinks-10.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-06_04_i-drinks-10.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.i] Probability of typically consuming zero drinks by age, with confidence intervals: it rises with age for both groups, from about 0.03 at 21 to 0.17 at 35 for men and from about 0.11 to 0.33 for women."}

## R

- In R, **plot_predictions** only predicts the expected count
  - Instead, use **predictions()** first and convert each person's predicted count to the probability of a specific count with **dpois(#, x)** inside the **hypothesis** option
    - Take the **mean()** to average within each age and gender combination
  - Use **ggplot** to make the graph using the stored predictions

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[6.4.i] Probability of typically consuming zero drinks by age, with confidence intervals: it rises with age for both groups, from about 0.03 at 21 to 0.17 at 35 for men and from about 0.11 to 0.33 for women."
# 6.4.i - Pr(y=0)
pr0 <- predictions(pmod, type = "response",
  newdata = datagrid(age = 21:35, woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  hypothesis = ~ I(mean(dpois(0, x))) | age + woman)

ggplot(pr0, aes(age, estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, color = woman, fill = woman)) +
  geom_ribbon(alpha = .2, color = NA) + geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(21, 35, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .4, .1), limits = c(0, .4)) +
  labs(title = "[6.4.i] Probability of Consuming Zero Drinks in a Typical Sitting",
    x = "Age in Years", y = "Pr(Typically Consumes 0 Drinks)", color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

:::

### Marginal effects on probabilities of specific counts

- Define $\eta$ as the probability of a specific count \# (or range)

$$\eta = \Pr(y = j\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \frac{e^{-\widehat{\mu}_{i}}\,\widehat{\mu}_{i}^{\,j}}{j!}$$

- Marginal effect is difference in probability of specific count, conditional on two values of the focal IV of interest

$$ME = \eta(x_{k} = end,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*}) - \eta(x_{k} = start,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*})$$

> ***Interpretation:** The difference in the probability of a count of \# for a change in x~k~ of δ, holding other independent variables constant*

- And for a range of counts

> ***Interpretation:** The difference in the probability of a count between \# and \# for a change in x~k~ of δ, holding other independent variables constant*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*NOTE: Pass customized predict() functions
mecompare age, model(pmod) amount(trimrange) predict(pr(0))
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
avg_comparisons(pmod, variables = list(age = c(26, 31)),
  comparison = function(hi, lo) dpois(0, hi) - dpois(0, lo))
```

:::

> *Aging from the 5^th^ to 95^th^ percentile in the data (26 to 31), predicts a 6.5 percentage point increase in the probability of not drinking any alcoholic drinks.*

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
**Interpretation tip**: As with a +SD effect, the first time you report a (trimmed) range ME, useful to remind readers what those values are in your data.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

- In R, for a range of counts, use **ppois(#, x)**, which gives the probability of \# or fewer. Specify amount between *end \#* and *start \# -- 1*. E.g. For Pr(*y* = 4--18)

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[6.4.k] Probability of typically consuming four or more drinks by age, with confidence intervals: it falls with age, from about 0.52 at 21 to 0.13 at 35 for men and from about 0.22 to 0.04 for women."
# 6.4.k - Pr(y >= 4)
pr4_18 <- predictions(pmod, type = "response",
  newdata = datagrid(age = 21:35, woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  hypothesis = ~ I(mean(ppois(18, x) - ppois(3, x))) | age + woman)

ggplot(pr4_18, aes(age, estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, color = woman, fill = woman)) +
  geom_ribbon(alpha = .2, color = NA) + geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(21, 35, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .7, .1), limits = c(0, .7)) +
  labs(title = "[6.4.k] Probability of Consuming Four or More Drinks in a Typical Sitting",
    x = "Age in Years", y = "Pr(Typically Consumes 4+ Drinks)", color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

:::

### Marginal effects on probability of a range of counts

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare age, model(pmod) amount(sd) predict(pr(4,18))
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
# Center changes in continuous IVs on each observation's value (as mecompare does)
options(marginaleffects_contrast_direction = "center")

avg_comparisons(pmod, variables = list(age = sd(ah4$age)),
  comparison = function(hi, lo) (ppois(18, hi) - ppois(3, hi)) - (ppois(18, lo) - ppois(3, lo)))
```

:::

> *In this article, we define **risk of alcohol misuse** as reporting an average number of alcoholic drinks in a sitting as 4 or more. Using this definition, aging a standard deviation (about 2 years) predicts a 3.5 percentage point decrease in the probability of being at risk of alcohol misuse.*
